Exercise 3.3 · Week 3

Top 3 High Scores

Python in Thonny Work in pairs

Goal: keep a list of scores and print only the best three.

Two new list tricks:

  • sorted(scores, reverse=True) makes a new list, biggest first.
  • best[:3] takes the first three items. If there are fewer, it takes them all.
  1. Open starter.py and press Run. The "top three" are not the best!
  2. TODO 1: sort first, then take three.
  3. TODO 2: print 1st: 300, 2nd: 120, 3rd: 80. Use the places list.

Done looks like:

1st: 300
2nd: 120
3rd: 80
What did you score this time? 500
New leaderboard:
1st: 500
2nd: 300
3rd: 120

Extra: store a made-up nickname with each score, e.g. print 1st: 300 (Comet).

Starter code

Open starter.py in Thonny, or copy the code below into a new file and save it as starter.py.

# Top 3 High Scores
# Keep a list of scores and show only the best three.


def add_score(scores, new_score):
    """Add a new score to the list and return the list."""
    scores.append(new_score)
    return scores


def top_three(scores):
    """Return the three highest scores, biggest first."""
    # TODO 1: this takes the first three, not the BEST three.
    # Sort a copy first:  best = sorted(scores, reverse=True)
    # then return best[:3]
    return scores[:3]


def print_leaderboard(scores):
    """Print the top three with 1st, 2nd and 3rd in front."""
    places = ["1st", "2nd", "3rd"]
    best = top_three(scores)
    # TODO 2: print each score with its place, like "1st: 300".
    # Tip: for i in range(len(best)):   then use places[i] and best[i]
    print(best)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    scores = [120, 45, 300, 80]
    print_leaderboard(scores)
    new_score = int(input("What did you score this time? "))
    add_score(scores, new_score)
    print("New leaderboard:")
    print_leaderboard(scores)

Stuck? Open a hint

Try on your own first. Hints open one at a time, from a small nudge to a bigger one. None of them gives the answer away.

Hint 1: Where to look

Run it and read what prints. The first three scores in the list are not the biggest three. Look at top_three first, then at how print_leaderboard shows the result.

Hint 2: Try this

sorted() puts a list in order and gives a new list. Add reverse=True to put the biggest first. Then [:3] keeps the first three. To print, loop with an index so you can pair each place name with its score.

Hint 3: Almost there

In top_three, write best = sorted(____, reverse=____), then return best[:____]. In print_leaderboard, use for i in range(len(____)): and print(f"{places[____]}: {best[____]}").
